work.title: The Life of King Henry the Fifth
work.author: William Shakespeare

scene.label: Act 5, Scene 1
scene.title: SCENE I. France. The English camp.

lines.text: Nay, that's right; but why wear you your leek today?
lines.plainText: Nay that's right but why wear you your leek today

lines.text: Saint Davy's day is past.
lines.plainText: Saint Davy's day is past

lines.text: There is occasions and causes why and wherefore in all things. I will tell you ass my friend, Captain Gower. The rascally, scald, beggarly, lousy, pragging knave, Pistol, which you and yourself and all the world know to be no petter than a fellow, look you now, of no merits, he is come to me and prings me pread and salt yesterday, look you, and bid me eat my leek. It was in a place where I could not breed no contention with him; but I will be so bold as to wear it in my cap till I see him once again, and then I will tell him a little piece of my desires.
lines.plainText: There is occasions and causes why and wherefore in all things I will tell you ass my friend Captain Gower The rascally scald beggarly lousy pragging knave Pistol which you and yourself and all the world know to be no petter than a fellow look you now of no merits he is come to me and prings me pread and salt yesterday look you and bid me eat my leek It was in a place where I could not breed no contention with him but I will be so bold as to wear it in my cap till I see him once again and then I will tell him a little piece of my desires

lines.text: Why, here he comes, swelling like a turkey-cock.
lines.plainText: Why here he comes swelling like a turkeycock

lines.text: 'Tis no matter for his swellings nor his turkey-cocks. God pless you, Anchient Pistol! you scurvy, lousy knave, God pless you!
lines.plainText: 'Tis no matter for his swellings nor his turkeycocks God pless you Anchient Pistol you scurvy lousy knave God pless you

lines.text: Ha! art thou bedlam? Dost thou thirst, base Trojan,
lines.plainText: Ha art thou bedlam Dost thou thirst base Trojan

lines.text: To have me fold up Parca's fatal web?
lines.plainText: To have me fold up Parca's fatal web

lines.text: Hence! I am qualmish at the smell of leek.
lines.plainText: Hence I am qualmish at the smell of leek

lines.text: I peseech you heartily, scurfy, lousy knave, at my desires, and my requests, and my petitions, to eat, look you, this leek. Because, look you, you do not love it, nor your affections and your appetites and your digestions does not agree with it, I would desire you to eat it.
lines.plainText: I peseech you heartily scurfy lousy knave at my desires and my requests and my petitions to eat look you this leek Because look you you do not love it nor your affections and your appetites and your digestions does not agree with it I would desire you to eat it

lines.text: Not for Cadwallader and all his goats.
lines.plainText: Not for Cadwallader and all his goats

lines.text: There is one goat for you. [Strikes him.] Will you be so good, scald knave, as eat it?
lines.plainText: There is one goat for you Strikes him Will you be so good scald knave as eat it

lines.text: Base Trojan, thou shalt die.
lines.plainText: Base Trojan thou shalt die

lines.text: You say very true, scald knave, when God's will is. I will desire you to live in the mean time, and eat your victuals. Come, there is sauce for it. [Strikes him.] You call'd me yesterday mountain-squire; but I will make you today a squire of low degree. I pray you, fall to; if you can mock a leek, you can eat a leek.
lines.plainText: You say very true scald knave when God's will is I will desire you to live in the mean time and eat your victuals Come there is sauce for it Strikes him You call'd me yesterday mountainsquire but I will make you today a squire of low degree I pray you fall to if you can mock a leek you can eat a leek

lines.text: Enough, captain; you have astonish'd him.
lines.plainText: Enough captain you have astonish'd him

lines.text: I say, I will make him eat some part of my leek, or I will peat his pate four days. Bite, I pray you; it is good for your green wound and your ploody coxcomb.
lines.plainText: I say I will make him eat some part of my leek or I will peat his pate four days Bite I pray you it is good for your green wound and your ploody coxcomb

lines.text: Must I bite?
lines.plainText: Must I bite

lines.text: Yes, certainly, and out of doubt and out of question too, and ambiguities.
lines.plainText: Yes certainly and out of doubt and out of question too and ambiguities

lines.text: By this leek, I will most horribly revenge. I eat and eat, I swear—
lines.plainText: By this leek I will most horribly revenge I eat and eat I swear

lines.text: Eat, I pray you. Will you have some more sauce to your leek? There is not enough leek to swear by.
lines.plainText: Eat I pray you Will you have some more sauce to your leek There is not enough leek to swear by

lines.text: Quiet thy cudgel; thou dost see I eat.
lines.plainText: Quiet thy cudgel thou dost see I eat

lines.text: Much good do you, scald knave, heartily. Nay, pray you, throw none away; the skin is good for your broken coxcomb. When you take occasions to see leeks hereafter, I pray you, mock at 'em; that is all.
lines.plainText: Much good do you scald knave heartily Nay pray you throw none away the skin is good for your broken coxcomb When you take occasions to see leeks hereafter I pray you mock at 'em that is all

lines.text: Good.
lines.plainText: Good

lines.text: Ay, leeks is good. Hold you, there is a groat to heal your pate.
lines.plainText: Ay leeks is good Hold you there is a groat to heal your pate

lines.text: Me a groat!
lines.plainText: Me a groat

lines.text: Yes, verily and in truth you shall take it; or I have another leek in my pocket, which you shall eat.
lines.plainText: Yes verily and in truth you shall take it or I have another leek in my pocket which you shall eat

lines.text: I take thy groat in earnest of revenge.
lines.plainText: I take thy groat in earnest of revenge

lines.text: If I owe you anything I will pay you in cudgels. You shall be a woodmonger, and buy nothing of me but cudgels. God be wi' you, and keep you, and heal your pate.
lines.plainText: If I owe you anything I will pay you in cudgels You shall be a woodmonger and buy nothing of me but cudgels God be wi' you and keep you and heal your pate

lines.text: All hell shall stir for this.
lines.plainText: All hell shall stir for this

lines.text: Go, go; you are a couterfeit cowardly knave. Will you mock at an ancient tradition, begun upon an honourable respect, and worn as a memorable trophy of predeceased valour, and dare not avouch in your deeds any of your words? I have seen you gleeking and galling at this gentleman twice or thrice. You thought, because he could not speak English in the native garb, he could not therefore handle an English cudgel. You find it otherwise; and henceforth let a Welsh correction teach you a good English condition. Fare ye well.
lines.plainText: Go go you are a couterfeit cowardly knave Will you mock at an ancient tradition begun upon an honourable respect and worn as a memorable trophy of predeceased valour and dare not avouch in your deeds any of your words I have seen you gleeking and galling at this gentleman twice or thrice You thought because he could not speak English in the native garb he could not therefore handle an English cudgel You find it otherwise and henceforth let a Welsh correction teach you a good English condition Fare ye well

lines.text: Doth Fortune play the huswife with me now?
lines.plainText: Doth Fortune play the huswife with me now

lines.text: News have I, that my Doll is dead i' the spital
lines.plainText: News have I that my Doll is dead i' the spital

lines.text: Of malady of France;
lines.plainText: Of malady of France

lines.text: And there my rendezvous is quite cut off.
lines.plainText: And there my rendezvous is quite cut off

lines.text: Old I do wax; and from my weary limbs
lines.plainText: Old I do wax and from my weary limbs

lines.text: Honour is cudgell'd. Well, bawd I'll turn,
lines.plainText: Honour is cudgell'd Well bawd I'll turn

lines.text: And something lean to cutpurse of quick hand.
lines.plainText: And something lean to cutpurse of quick hand

lines.text: To England will I steal, and there I'll steal;
lines.plainText: To England will I steal and there I'll steal

lines.text: And patches will I get unto these cudgell'd scars,
lines.plainText: And patches will I get unto these cudgell'd scars

lines.text: And swear I got them in the Gallia wars.
lines.plainText: And swear I got them in the Gallia wars
